Newly hatched larvae of the Siberian salamander (Salamandrella keyserlingii) emerge from their gelatinous egg masses at a remarkably small size, with individuals measuring just 3 centimeters  in snout-vent length at metamorphosis. This diminutive stage is sustained endogenously during the early lecithotrophic phase, drawing upon a modest yolk reserve. The wet weight at birth is correspondingly low, recorded at 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams], a value that reflects the initial energetic capital contained within each egg before exogenous feeding commences. The transition to active foraging begins shortly after the onset of aquatic larval life, during which the free-swimming tadpoles graze on detritus and microinvertebrates. Growth during this pre-metamorphic interval is rapid, but the pace is heavily influenced by water temperature. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 12 °C [T = 12 °C], larvae progress through successive developmental stages, and body mass accumulation accelerates as the gill-breathing juveniles approach the morphological transformation that precedes their eventual terrestrial phase.

Sexual maturation in Salamandrella keyserlingii occurs after individuals have attained a sufficient body size, which differs markedly between the sexes. Field surveys indicate that females typically reach puberty at a snout-vent length of 6.12 centimeters [Lp = 6.12 centimeters], whereas males achieve reproductive maturity at a slightly smaller body size, with puberty recorded at 5.76 centimeters [Lp = 5.76 centimeters]. This divergence in size at maturity is a common pattern among urodeles and is often attributed to the energetic demands of oogenesis, which require a larger somatic frame to accommodate yolk deposition. The onset of gonadal maturation in females is accompanied by the development of the characteristic egg sacs that define the breeding season. Reproductively active adults are most frequently encountered in early spring, shortly after ice melt in the Siberian permafrost regions, when they migrate to shallow temporary ponds. The timing of these reproductive migrations is tightly linked to thermal cues, as the species is adapted to short, cold growing seasons typical of its high-latitude distribution.

Reproductive output in the Siberian salamander is characterized by a single annual breeding event, during which females deposit approximately 200 eggs contained within two gelatinous sacs [N_R_i = approximately 200 eggs contained within two gelatinous sacs]. This clutch represents the entirety of the yearly reproductive effort, as individuals produce only one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year] under typical environmental conditions. The eggs are attached to submerged vegetation, where they develop over several weeks. Field observations conducted at sites where water temperature remains near 12 °C [T = 12 °C] confirm that this thermal regime supports the highest observed rates of reproductive activity. The eggs are laid in a single sizable clutch each season, rather than multiple smaller clutches, maximizing the reproductive rate under these conditions. The gelatinous egg masses serve a protective function, shielding the developing embryos from microbial infection and buffering against abrupt temperature fluctuations. Hatching synchrony within a clutch is generally high, with most larvae emerging within a narrow temporal window that coincides with peak zooplankton abundance in the breeding ponds.

The ultimate body size of adult Siberian salamanders shows a consistent pattern of sexual dimorphism, with females attaining a larger maximum snout-vent length than males. The ultimate snout-vent length for females reaches 7 centimeters [Li = 7 centimeters], while males achieve a somewhat smaller ultimate size of 6.5 centimeters [Li = 6.5 centimeters]. This size discrepancy is not unusual among hynobiid salamanders, where larger female body size is thought to confer a fecundity advantage by allowing for the production of larger or more numerous egg clutches. The total body length of the species, including the tail, has been reported to reach up to 12.5 centimeters, which places Salamandrella keyserlingii among the medium-sized members of its family. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult has been estimated at 3.8 grams [Wwi = 3.8 grams], a value that reflects the modest overall body mass of this slender, cold-adapted amphibian. This relatively light body mass is consistent with the species' reliance on rapid bursts of activity during the brief active season followed by prolonged periods of inactivity during the harsh winter months.

Maximum documented longevity in this species provides an instructive window into its life-history strategy, which is characterized by a slow pace of life relative to many other amphibians of similar body size. Under stable conditions in captivity, with individuals maintained at a constant temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the oldest recorded individuals have survived for 10 years [am = 10 years]. This extended lifespan, equivalent to over 3,650 days, is notable for a urodele of such modest dimensions and is likely an adaptation to the highly unpredictable and resource-limited environments of the Siberian taiga and tundra. The ability to postpone reproduction across multiple seasons and to survive years of poor conditions before a successful breeding event is a hallmark of a bet-hedging life history. Natural mortality in the wild is presumably higher, primarily driven by predation from aquatic insects, fish, and birds during the aquatic larval stage. Despite these pressures, the combination of a small initial size and a long potential reproductive window allows Siberian salamander populations to persist across their vast geographic range, from northeastern European Russia to Kamchatka and Japan.
